item.title: Solana remains mostly rangebound as the negative macro backdrop limits the recovery. What's next?
item.description:
Solana has been consolidating near recent lows as the crypto market remains under pressure from tightening financial conditions. There has been some broad short-covering, but no positive catalyst backing the move.

Keep in mind that cryptocurrencies are very sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk sentiment, so higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions tend to be strong bearish drivers.

In terms of macro fundamentals, the picture remains largely unchanged. The Fed is still expected to raise rates, with the extent of tightening depending on incoming economic data and stock market conditions. The prolonged US-Iran stalemate is another source of uncertainty, keeping energy prices and inflation risks elevated while weighing on future growth expectations.

On the Solana-specific front, there haven’t been major developments after the network completed the Alpenglow consensus upgrade in October.

Looking ahead, the upside in Solana will likely remain limited as long as macro conditions remain unfavourable. A sustained recovery will likely require a more dovish Fed or a breakthrough in the US-Iran situation as would improve global growth expectations.

If we get a pullback into the major downward trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting the 60.00 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the 98.00 level next.

item.title: Connecting the dots: When does the AI selloff become a Fed problem?
item.description:
At what point does Nvidia's falling share price become the Fed's headache?

Now, wait a second. That sounds a little silly, doesn't it? But given how much of the US economic growth story is riding on AI these days, I wouldn't laugh off that question so easily.

Let's say you have made a decent amount of money from the stock market over the past few years. You're feeling a little richer and perhaps more comfortable about booking that family holiday or even splurging on a new car. But out of nowhere, a good chunk of those gains disappears in just a matter of weeks. Suddenly, that old car doesn't look so bad after all now, does it?

Economists call this the wealth effect. And you don't necessarily have to sell your stocks to change your spending habits. Just the notion of feeling poorer can be enough. And while stock market wealth is largely concentrated among the richer households, a prolonged selloff could still take some of the shine off US consumer spending as a whole.

This is where the AI boom also puts food on a lot more tables than we might realise.

Take for example building a data centre. It isn't just about buying a truckload of Nvidia chips. You need construction workers, electricians, cooling equipment, power supplies and plenty of other things. Just think that there are entire businesses banking on the assumption that the tech giants will keep spending as aggressively as they have been.

Now, a falling share price alone probably won't persuade Microsoft or Amazon to abandon their AI ambitions. But if those investments aren't making as much money as promised, shareholders might become a little less forgiving. And not everyone in the AI business has deep pockets. It's one thing to build a data centre with money you've already earned, but it's a whole other thing to borrow millions today on the assumption that you'll make enough money from AI tomorrow. So if lenders start questioning those assumptions, they might demand higher interest rates or become less willing to lend altogether.

All of a sudden, a data centre project that made perfect financial sense six months ago might no longer be worth pursuing. And the Fed wouldn't have needed to raise interest rates by a single basis point for that to happen.

In continuing to see how all of this is trickling down, fewer projects mean fewer orders. And that means a supplier might hold off hiring more workers, while a contractor might find itself having to let some people go.

In turn, those workers might spend less at restaurants, shops and other businesses that have absolutely nothing to do with AI. In essence, nobody needs to lose their life savings for an AI bust to hurt the economy.

Can you see where all of this is going now?

Typically, weaker consumer spending and a softer jobs market would strengthen the case for the Fed to lower interest rates. However, we are being caught in a higher for longer backdrop now with inflation pressures looking quite unforgiving. And that is even discounting the fact that the AI productivity miracle that was supposed to help businesses produce more at a lower cost looks to be taking longer to materialise.

As such, we could end up with weaker economic growth without quite the same relief on inflation. And that would leave policymakers at the Fed in a rather uncomfortable spot.

The Fed doesn't have a mandate to protect your stock portfolio. It does, however, have one to support employment and maintain price stability. And that's why traders should not only be concerned about how much further tech stocks might fall. They should really be worried about how much of the economy might get dragged down with tech stocks if the selling continues.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil extends the rebound as growth concerns ease and US-Iran tensions provide support
item.description:

On the news front, Trump touted the US naval blockade and continued military deployment while saying that Washington is still giving Iran an opportunity to reach an agreement. He also threatened to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain if no deal is reached.

item.title: Germany unemployment rises more than expected in November as labour market struggles persist
item.description:
• Germany November unemployment change 9k vs 4k expected
  • Prior 4k
  • Germany November unemployment rate 6.4% vs 6.4% expected
  • Prior 6.4%

The number of people out of work in Germany rose by more than expected in November, though the jobless rate is seen holding steady on the month at 6.4%. Overall, the total number of unemployed persons rose to 3.025 million in seasonally adjusted terms.

But when looking at the unadjusted total, it fell by 19,000 to 2.936 million in November with the labour office noting that the decline reflected the end of the autumn seasonal pickup. However, I'd put more weight on the seasonally adjusted figures here as they strip out the usual seasonal fluctuations and offer a better indication of the underlying health of the labour market.

As for the overall report, the labour office noted that "the trend of recent months is continuing" and that "the slight economic recovery has not led to revival in the labour market in November".

If you couple that with the subdued consumer confidence figures yesterday, then you can see why there are still concerns about the sustainability of the recovery. If households become more worried about job security, they're more likely to hold back on spending. That will then give businesses even less incentive to expand and hire.

In turn, it also makes life more complicated for the ECB, which is still having to contend with elevated inflation despite pockets of economic weakness across the region.

Looking to next year, I'd keep a close eye on whether the weakness in hiring starts to translate into more widespread job cuts. A more sluggish labour market is one thing but a more pronounced deterioration in employment could make Germany's economic recovery considerably harder to sustain.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stock market open: The rebound party rolls on
item.description:
• Eurostoxx +1.1%
  • Germany DAX +0.7%
  • France CAC 40 +0.4%
  • UK FTSE +0.7%
  • Spain IBEX +0.9%
  • Italy FTSE MIB +1.5%

It looks like dip buyers are hoping to squeeze in a little bit of joy out of what has otherwise been a rather miserable month for equities.

European stocks are building on yesterday's impressive gains, while S&P 500 futures are now up 1.8% and Nasdaq futures up 2.5%. Tech shares are once again leading the charge, which is encouraging considering that they have been at the heart of much of the market's troubles this month.

European investors already had a chance to celebrate Wednesday's turnaround on Wall Street during the Thanksgiving holiday yesterday. So, today's gains are more about extending that optimism as US traders return to their desks later in the day.

My only reservation is that we're heading into what will be an abbreviated trading session in the US, with the Thanksgiving holiday still somewhat hanging over. That means we will see thinner liquidity conditions and potential month-end flows also in play.

As such, lesser market participants will mean less money to move markets and so the size of any rally today might not necessarily reflect the strength of conviction behind it.

If anything else, I reckon the main focus will be on whether tech shares can hold on to their gains after the opening bell and whether the buying extends to other corners of the market. At this stage, a broader recovery would be far more encouraging than another tech-led bounce alone.

For now at least, dip buyers have the upper hand at the European market open. However, next week should offer a much better test of whether this recovery has legs. That is once liquidity conditions normalise and we put any shenanigans from November's portfolio rebalancing behind us.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Spanish inflation comes off the boil in November, offering some respite for the ECB
item.description:
• Spain November preliminary CPI +4.1% vs +4.6% y/y expected
  • Prior +4.9%
  • Spain November preliminary HICP +4.1% vs +4.7% y/y expected
  • Prior +4.9%

Much like the French report earlier, Spain's inflation numbers are also seen cooling off in November. After nearly hitting 5% in October, headline annual inflation is seen dropping back to 4.1% this month. The added good news is that core annual inflation was also estimated to drop to 2.6% in November, as compared to the 3.1% reading in the month before.

That being said, these figures are all still too high for any comfort for the ECB. And that's the troubling part for the central bank as they are dealing with quite an array of inflation backdrops across the region at this stage.

But as a whole, policymakers are arguably very much concerned about the risks of potential second-round effects. So, that remains the priority in terms of policy setting.

As things stand, they are likely to be able to get away with another rate hike in December. And the market pricing reflects roughly 93% odds of a 25 bps move already. But in looking to next year, the challenge will be how the central bank balances any further tightening measures against slowing economic growth.

The fiscal risks from France and now more trouble from US tariffs will make things even more challenging for the ECB. So, therein lies their predicament as we move to the final stages of the year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France inflation undershoots estimates in November as energy and services price pressures ease
item.description:
• France November preliminary CPI +2.9% vs +3.2% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.4%
  • France November preliminary HICP +3.2% vs +3.6% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.7%

Well, that's some good news for the French economy as inflation pressures are seen cooling back a little in November. The drop here is even below analyst estimates, with headline annual inflation dropping back below 3%. The monthly reading also shows that French inflation should ease by 0.7% in November, after having risen by 0.4% in October.

Looking at the details, energy inflation falling off is a key factor driving that development. Of note, energy prices are seen rising by 19.2% in November compared to the 24.1% increase in October.

That being said, core prices are also likely to come off the boil as services inflation cooled as well. Services prices were seen down to 2.3% in November compared to 2.6% in the month before.

All in all, the ECB can take some comfort in that as this will reduce stagflationary risks in Europe's second-largest economy. But even then, price pressures are admittedly still on the higher side and policymakers cannot rest on their laurels just yet.

For now, all of this still supports the argument that they may perhaps get away with another rate hike. But after, they will have to seriously consider the balance of risks between overtightening monetary policy and the necessity to tame the inflation monster amid potential second-round effects.

In other words, they will still be in a tough spot in trying to decide on policy so as to risk sending the economy off the ledge or allowing inflation pressures to grow to be too overwhelming. That will be the key challenge for policymakers next year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France Q3 GDP revised lower as economic woes deepen
item.description:
• France Q3 final GDP -0.2% vs -0.1% q/q prelim
  • Prior 0.0%

Ouch. France was already the troubling spot in the euro area and the negative revision to the preliminary GDP estimates only continues to underscore that notion. In volume terms, the French economy contracted by 0.2% in Q3 following some tentative stability in the previous quarter.

Domestic demand was pretty much subdued, stagnating on the quarter, while inventory changes contributed to 0.3% to quarterly GDP with net foreign trade being the main drag with a negative contribution of 0.6% on the quarter.

Overall, the French economy is seen growing by just 0.1% so far this year and that is hardly encouraging for Europe's second-largest economy.

As such, this won't steer the conversation away from stagflationary risks as we head into next year. The only good news is that the latest French inflation numbers for November is at least showing some signs of cooling, affording the ECB some added breathing room in looking to the French economy as a whole.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US reportedly urged Venezuela, Iraq to consider quitting OPEC earlier this year
item.description:
US president Trump has never been much of a fan of OPEC. And as it would seem, he'd quite like a few of its members to feel the same way.

In an exclusive report by Reuters today, the US administration is said to have encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to contemplate leaving OPEC earlier this year. Washington reportedly even blocked Venezuela's annual membership payment, while Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened over the summer to persuade the US to back off.

Despite such actions, the US State Department has maintained that an OPEC exit was not raised at senior levels with Venezuela and that discussions with Iraq centred on energy infrastructure. Sure, sure.

Now, this is all very on brand for Trump given his longstanding disdain for OPEC and the bloc's influence over oil prices. However, there is also arguably a commercial angle here. If Washington wants US oil companies to ramp up production in both countries, why have a third party dictating how much oil they can pump out of the ground?

Having said all that, the political realities are a little more complicated though.

For Venezuela, which is currently exempt from OPEC production quotas, walking away offers little to no immediate benefit. They would essentially be giving up its seat at the table before their oil industry has even fully recovered.

Meanwhile, Iraq's oil ministry has maintained that their position is more in favour of negotiating a bigger production allowance over leaving the bloc altogether. And there's merit to that stance. I mean, why surrender your bargaining power within the group when the very threat of leaving might help to secure a better deal?

As for what this means to the oil market, let's not be mistaken that these two countries leaving OPEC doesn't magically bring millions of additional barrels to market. It will still take much investment, infrastructure and time.

Trump's push here is mostly to try and trigger a snowball effect, particularly after the UAE's departure earlier this year. But for now, he's not going to get it his way on this one.

Circling back to the oil market, the OPEC+ meeting on 29 November this weekend will be a key risk event in seeing if the bloc can continue to keep its members' individual production ambitions aligned with its collective interest in supporting oil prices.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Reminder: Wall Street is back today but will dip buyers have the last laugh?
item.description:
It looks like dip buyers are coming back from their Thanksgiving dinner with quite the appetite. US futures are storming higher so far today, with S&P 500 futures up 1.8% and Nasdaq futures up a whopping 2.8% as tech shares look to end a bruising week on a brighter note.

After the impressive turnaround on Wednesday, there is a growing sense of optimism that dip buyers might finally be getting somewhere. However, the key question to end the week is whether they keep the party going when Wall Street returns later today?

As a reminder, US markets will only be open for an abbreviated trading session today. Both the NYSE and Nasdaq will close at 1800 GMT (1pm ET), three hours earlier than usual. Meanwhile, the bond market will close at 1900 GMT (2pm ET) before we break for the weekend.

Even with markets reopening though, I would expect liquidity conditions to remain rather patchy at best. Many market participants tend to take an extended break through the Thanksgiving weekend, so there might not necessarily be the usual crowd on Wall Street to greet dip buyers. But why should that matter?

In essence, fewer market players means that it will take less money to move prices. And that can make rallies look far more convincing than they really are, while also leaving the door open to some rather nasty and sudden reversals potentially. So, just be wary of that.

In looking to broader market sentiment today, I reckon the bigger test will be whether tech shares can build on the early gains once the cash market opens. The recovery on Wednesday showed that dip buyers were willing to step in at lower levels, but it's a different game altogether in trying to extend the buying and build back a more bullish appetite.

And when you throw in some potential month-end positioning ahead of Monday, it becomes even trickier to separate genuine buying conviction from temporary flows.

I'd certainly welcome a strong finish to the week after all the recent carnage and bloodbath in markets. But before getting too carried away, we also have to remind ourselves of the risks that are still present beyond the numbers on the screens.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold begins to find its feet again but are buyers out of the woods yet?
item.description:
Gold buyers have at least something to be thankful for this week. After a rather brutal month as a whole, the precious metal is finding a bit of a reprieve today as it pushes back above $3,600.

The question now though is how much should we really read into the latest bounce over the past few sessions?

Looking at the weekly chart, the $3,500 mark is proving to be a decent area for buyers to make a stand despite a brief slip below on Wednesday. And for the time being at least, buyers are also managing to nudge price back above the 50.0 Fib retracement level of the rally since 2022 - seen at around $3,608.

Now, those are some encouraging signals but the technical damage from breaking below the 100-week moving average (red line) earlier this month is still very much intact.

That being said, there is something a little more promising on the hourly chart today.

Gold has finally broken above its 100-hour moving average (red line), which has repeatedly kept buyers in check earlier this week. This is the first time in three weeks that the near-term bias is no longer siding with sellers. As such, that is giving buyers some momentum to work with in looking to the 200-hour moving average (blue line) at around $3,665 as the next key near-term hurdle. If buyers can move above that, then there is a stronger argument that the immediate selling pressure is starting to subside.

However, I still have my reservations when it comes to the latest bounce we're seeing here. Even as a gold bull myself, I wouldn't want to get too carried away considering the timing of the bounce this week.

While the broader risk mood is starting to look more upbeat again with US futures pointing higher, let's not forget the fact that we are potentially also getting caught in between month-end rebalancing flows and thinner liquidity conditions over the Thanksgiving holiday period. As such, I'm not sure I'd put too much stock in today's moves just yet.

Don't get me wrong. The technicals are definitely something one shouldn't ignore. However, I'd much rather see how gold fares when traders return to their desks next week and if there is appetite to hold any key near-term breaks today.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

  • US equity futures rallied, with Nasdaq 100 futures up about 2.4%, and Korean chip stocks led Asia higher, with the Kosdaq up around 6.7%
  • Tokyo core CPI rose to a 16-month high of 2.9%, keeping a December BoJ hike in play, though the BoJ's trend gauge eased to 2.5%

Markets overview Risk appetite improved through the Asian session on Friday after a bruising week for AI-linked assets. US equity index futures led the way, with Nasdaq 100 futures up about 2.4% and S&P 500 futures about 1.7% higher. South Korea's chip-heavy markets were the standout in Asia: the Kosdaq jumped around 6.7% and the Kospi gained close to 4%, as SK Hynix rose about 4.6% and Samsung Electronics about 4.2%. Japan's Nikkei 225 added around 1.9% to near 58,600, and the Topix rose about 1.8%. Gains in China were more modest, with the Hang Seng up around 0.9% and the Shanghai Composite edging up about 0.3%. US 10-year Treasury yields rose about 7 basis points to around 4.91%.

Japan Tokyo's core inflation rate climbed to 2.9% in November, its fastest pace in 16 months, from 2.6% in October, although it came in just below the 3.0% forecast. The Bank of Japan's preferred trend measure, which excludes fresh food and energy, eased to 2.5% from 2.6%, suggesting energy accounted for much of the rise. The data keep a December rate hike as the base case, with markets expecting the BoJ to lift its policy rate to 1.5% at its December 17-18 meeting. Nationwide CPI arrives only hours before that decision. USD/JPY was little changed near 159.20, while the two-year JGB yield held near 1.76%.

Australia and New Zealand The US dollar softened against the antipodean currencies, with AUD/USD up about 0.35% to around 0.6660 and NZD/USD up about 0.3% to around 0.5485.

The IMF urged the Reserve Bank of Australia to stand ready to raise rates further if inflation proves persistent, citing risks from Middle East energy prices and the danger of inflation expectations becoming unanchored. It also pressed the government to deliver on spending restraint. OCBC took a different view, arguing that the RBA is close to the end of its tightening cycle as the labour market softens, and that the Australian dollar's upside will be increasingly capped as Australia's rate advantage narrows.

In New Zealand, official election results confirmed a hung parliament, with the centre-right coalition needing the centrist Opportunity Party to govern. The currency market took the result in its stride. Earlier, New Zealand consumer confidence rose to 100.2, its highest since January, as falling fuel prices eased inflation expectations.

China China's cabinet pledged new incremental policies for its capital markets, a stronger role for the state-backed national team in stabilising stocks, tighter defences against imported risks, and more dividends and buybacks from listed companies. It gave no details on the size or timing of the support. Industrial profits rose 20.1% from a year earlier in October, up from 14.4% in September, but the gains were concentrated in electronics, with weak household demand and the property downturn still weighing on consumer-facing industries.

Gold and commodities Gold rebounded about 1.9% to around $3,630 an ounce, rising even as US yields climbed, while silver jumped nearly 5% to around $43. Views on the metal remain divided. HSBC warned that further equity weakness could push gold through major support at $3,400, while Saxo's Ole Hansen pointed to signs of selling exhaustion. Commonwealth Bank of Australia said the dollar, already near its expected peak, will drive gold in the coming months, and it sees limited downside, with a year-end range of $3,500 to $3,700. Separately, the Reserve Bank of India bought no gold in the six months to September but moved about 60 tonnes home from overseas vaults.

Oil edged higher, with Brent up about 0.7% to around $92 a barrel and WTI up about 1% to near $86. OCBC expects the rupee to strengthen as oil eases, forecasting USD/INR at 92.10 by the end of 2027.

Also on our radar SpaceX will issue new Class A stock to every US child with an active Trump Account, and Elon Musk pledged to personally match the gift once his lockup ends in June, doubling last month's pledge as total program deposits passed $9 billion. CNBC later reported that SpaceX shares rose on an alternative trading platform. Bitcoin rose almost 1% to around $61,500, after JPMorgan flagged a record discount at Strategy as a possible capitulation signal. item.title: Five steps from China's cabinet to shore up its stock market, but no numbers yet
item.description:
The pledges should help put a floor under mainland equities, as investors tend to front-run state buying once the national team is explicitly mentioned. The follow-through will depend on whether concrete funding and specific measures follow from the securities regulator. Hong Kong-listed Chinese shares and China-sensitive currencies, including the yuan and Australian dollar, may get some support from improved sentiment. The warning on imported risks suggests Beijing sees global AI-related equity volatility as the main threat, so mainland stocks may stay partly insulated from Wall Street swings. Without new figures, though, any rally could fade quickly if global selling resumes.

---

Beijing has signalled it is ready to defend its stock market, with the cabinet pledging new policies, a bigger role for state-backed buyers and more shareholder payouts, though it gave no details on the size or timing of support.

Summary:

  • China's State Council pledged to implement existing policies and plan new incremental measures for capital markets
  • It vowed to strengthen the role of the state-backed "national team" in stabilising the market
  • Officials will further improve stock market stabilisation mechanisms
  • The cabinet pledged to strengthen defences against imported risks in capital markets
  • Listed companies will be pushed to increase dividends and share buybacks
  • No details were given on the size or timing of new measures

China's cabinet has pledged to roll out new incremental policies for its capital markets and to give state-backed investors a bigger role in steadying share prices. The move signals Beijing's readiness to defend its stock market as global turmoil in AI-linked stocks spills over into Asia.

A State Council meeting on Friday agreed to implement existing policies while planning new incremental measures for the capital market, state news agency Xinhua reported. Officials pledged to strengthen the role of the so-called "national team" in stabilising markets, further improve the stock market's stabilisation mechanisms, and step up efforts to guard against imported risks in capital markets.

The national team is the group of state-backed funds and financial institutions that buy shares, often through exchange-traded funds, when markets come under heavy selling pressure. Beijing has relied on them repeatedly during past selloffs. An explicit pledge to expand their role is among the clearest signals officials can send that they are prepared to put a floor under prices.

The reference to imported risks is notable. It suggests policymakers are increasingly worried that the volatility rattling global equity markets, driven by doubts over the AI investment boom and the risk of further Federal Reserve rate hikes, could feed into Chinese markets through foreign investor flows and sentiment.

The cabinet also said it would push listed companies to increase dividends and share buybacks. That's part of a longer-running effort to make Chinese stocks more attractive to long-term investors by improving shareholder returns, an area where mainland firms have often lagged their global peers.

The meeting gave no details on the size or timing of any new measures. Its wording promises to plan new policies rather than announcing specific steps, which leaves markets waiting for follow-up action from the securities regulator and other agencies.

The pledges come against a mixed economic backdrop. Data on Friday showed profits at industrial firms rose 20.1% from a year earlier in October, but the gains were concentrated in electronics, while weak household demand and the property downturn continued to weigh on consumer-facing sectors. Supporting the stock market can help household wealth and confidence, which policymakers see as important for reviving domestic consumption.

Previous rounds of verbal support have often lifted Chinese shares in the short term, but sustained gains have usually depended on concrete funding commitments and evidence of stronger growth. Investors will be watching for details on how much firepower the national team will get, and how quickly. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Warsh's 2018 dilemma returns as an AI stock rout meets a Fed bent on taming inflation
item.description:
The message for equity investors is that the bar for Fed support is much higher than in 2018. With core inflation at 3.3%, an orderly decline in AI-linked stocks is more likely to be treated as useful tightening than as a reason to pause. That keeps a December hike firmly priced and supports the dollar and short-dated Treasury yields. The key signal is the Fed's December projections, which are expected to show more hikes ahead. Credit markets are the trigger to watch: stress among heavily indebted AI-related borrowers would be far more likely to shift the Fed's stance than falling share prices alone. For gold, which pays no yield, a Fed still focused on hiking remains a headwind.

---

Kevin Warsh once urged the Fed to back off as stocks slid in 2018, but with inflation stuck well above target and AI demand running hot, his Fed looks far more willing to let a market rout do some of its work.

Summary:

  • The AI-driven stock selloff could force Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh to choose between hiking rates and letting markets tighten conditions for him
  • Warsh urged the Fed to pause during the December 2018 selloff, when inflation was only just at target
  • Core PCE inflation rose to 3.3% in October from 3.1%, and has been above target for more than five years
  • Fed officials increasingly see AI-driven demand as a source of persistent price pressure
  • Markets expect a hike at the December 8-9 meeting, with officials divided on how far to go after that
  • A disorderly selloff, especially in credit tied to more than $800 billion of AI-related debt, remains the bigger concern

The rout in AI-linked stocks is testing how much market turmoil the Federal Reserve is willing to tolerate in its fight against inflation, and so far the answer appears to be a lot. If the selloff deepens, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh may have to choose between delivering on his tough talk on prices and relying on falling markets to do some of the tightening for him.

As Nick Timiraos reported in The Wall Street Journal (gated), Warsh has faced this dilemma before, from the outside. In December 2018, with stocks about 11% below their peak, he co-wrote a piece urging the Fed to pause its tightening. The Fed hiked anyway, the selloff accelerated into the worst December for stocks since 1931, and officials quickly signalled they were in no rush to move again.

The parallels with today are striking. Then, as now, a first-year Fed chair was raising rates into falling stocks and a stronger dollar, during a geopolitical shock and after a midterm setback for President Trump, who opposed tighter policy. The crucial difference is inflation. In 2018 it had only just reached the Fed's 2% target. Today it has been above target for more than five years, and Warsh, who took over in May, has said the Fed will not accept inflation that stays even modestly above 2%.

That leaves little room for a 2019-style retreat. Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy, rose to 3.3% in October from 3.1% in September, well up from a low of 2.6% in March 2025, before broad US tariffs took effect. Fed officials are increasingly worried that AI is driving a surge in demand that, unlike an oil or tariff shock, will not fade on its own. New York Fed President John Williams has said his main concern is the strength of AI-related demand rather than past supply shocks.

Some see the market slide as part of the cure rather than a problem. Lower stock prices are one of the channels through which higher rates slow spending. Former Boston Fed President Eric Rosengren put it bluntly: "If you want to slow down the economy, you have to slow down AI investment." Officials are also wary of reinforcing the "Fed put", the belief that the central bank will cushion every selloff.

That does not mean markets are irrelevant. A sustained decline would weigh on household spending and make it harder for companies to raise money, which could reduce how far the Fed needs to go. Williams has said a material and sustained change in financial conditions would affect his outlook, but he saw recent swings as volatility rather than a fundamental reassessment of AI. A disorderly selloff is the bigger worry, especially in credit. Michelle Bowman, the Fed's Vice Chair for Supervision, has said AI-related debt is on track to top $800 billion this year, with off-balance-sheet commitments estimated at more than three times that.

Investors overwhelmingly expect another hike at the December 8-9 meeting, after the Fed raised rates in September. The debate is over what comes next. Some officials could favour stopping after one more move if falling commodity prices ease inflation. Others take a more hawkish view. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has argued that three more hikes next year could be warranted, and Williams has not ruled out consecutive increases.

Warsh's own record offers mixed signals. He has long argued the Fed should pay more attention to market prices than to lagging data. Yet in October 2018 he said the Fed should not fret over a 10% drop in stocks, only to call for a pause ten weeks later. How he weighs a deeper rout against stubborn inflation may become the defining test of his early tenure.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Aussie upside capped as jobless rate hits 4.9% and the RBA nears its peak, OCBC says
item.description:
For AUD/USD, OCBC's view points to selling into rallies rather than chasing a risk-led bounce, although the currency is likely to stay highly sensitive to equity swings. The December 8 RBA decision is the key event risk. Any hint of further tightening would challenge the capped-upside view, while a clearly neutral message would support it. The cross rates may show the rate story more clearly than the dollar pair: if other central banks keep tightening while the RBA holds, the Aussie could underperform against those currencies. Monthly jobs and inflation data will decide which side of the RBA debate wins out.

---

  • IMF tells RBA to stand ready for more hikes, even after 125bp of tightening this year

---

OCBC thinks the Australian dollar can bounce when risk appetite returns, but with the RBA close to done and the jobs market weakening, it sees Australia's rate advantage fading and the Aussie's upside increasingly capped.

Summary:

  • OCBC expects the AUD's upside to be increasingly capped, even if risk sentiment stabilises
  • The RBA is seen as close to the end of its tightening cycle, while other central banks still have room to catch up
  • October inflation picked up, with headline CPI at 4.9% y/y and trimmed mean at 3.8%
  • Employment fell by 43,500 in October, the second straight decline, and unemployment rose to a five-year high of 4.9%
  • OCBC sees a prolonged RBA hold, with a first rate cut in 4Q27 as its base case
  • The IMF and Citigroup see risks of further RBA hikes, setting up a clear policy debate

The Australian dollar may struggle to stage a lasting recovery even if global risk sentiment improves, according to OCBC. The bank argues that a softening labour market and a Reserve Bank of Australia nearing the end of its tightening cycle will gradually erode the currency's rate advantage.

The Aussie has been under pressure from the risk-off mood gripping markets, as turmoil in AI-linked stocks weighs on pro-cyclical currencies. OCBC said in its daily market outlook that the currency could rebound as sentiment stabilises, but it expects any upside to be increasingly capped.

The bank's case rests on relative interest rates. The RBA has raised its cash rate to 4.85%, the highest in 18 years, after five hikes this year. OCBC thinks the RBA is now close to done, while other central banks still have room to catch up. As they do, Australia's yield advantage, a key source of support for the currency, is likely to narrow.

The domestic data send mixed signals. Inflation is moving the wrong way: headline consumer prices rose 4.9% from a year earlier in October, up from 4.3%, while the trimmed mean measure of underlying inflation climbed to 3.8% from 3.6%. But the labour market is weakening. Employment fell by 43,500 in October, the second straight monthly decline, and unemployment rose to a five-year high of 4.9%.

That leaves the RBA caught between sticky inflation and softening jobs. OCBC believes the bar for further tightening is now high and expects a prolonged hold, with a first rate cut in the fourth quarter of 2027 as its base case. For the Australian dollar, that implies any rebound driven by improving risk sentiment is likely to lack staying power.

Not everyone sees the RBA as finished. The International Monetary Fund said on Friday that the central bank should stand ready to raise rates further if inflation proves persistent. Citigroup warned that surging AI-related business investment has pushed domestic demand above the economy's potential, keeping the risk of further hikes alive.

The RBA's next policy decision is due on December 8. A hawkish surprise there would challenge OCBC's view, while further weakness in the jobs market would reinforce it. Until then, the Aussie looks likely to trade on global risk appetite, with domestic rate expectations limiting how far it can climb. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: SpaceX and Musk to hand shares to every child holding an active Trump Account
item.description:
For existing SpaceX shareholders, the company's portion is newly issued Class A stock, so it means some dilution. How much depends on how many of the nearly 70 million accounts count as active, a number the company hasn't given. Musk's matching shares come from his own holdings and won't move until his lockup ends in June, so they add no new stock. More broadly, this is an interpretation rather than a stated fact: with deposits now above $9 billion, Trump Accounts look set to become a recognised channel for corporate and billionaire giving, which may push other high-profile companies to make pledges of their own. Over time, putting even a small stake in millions of children's hands could also widen SpaceX's retail ownership base well beyond its traditional investor pool.

--- SpaceX and Musk are using Trump Accounts to put a slice of the rocket maker into the hands of millions of American children, doubling his earlier pledge as the program grows past $9 billion.

Summary:

  • SpaceX will issue new Class A common shares to every American child with an active Trump Account, and Musk will personally match the company's gift
  • The move doubles a pledge Musk made last month; SpaceX's shares are due to be distributed next month, Musk's when his lockup expires in June next year
  • SpaceX President and COO Gwynne Shotwell has separately pledged more than 2 million shares for children aged 11 to 17 in low-income areas, mainly near her home in central Texas
  • Friends and family have contributed over $1 billion to individual accounts, taking total program deposits above $9 billion
  • Nearly 70 million accounts are open, more than 60 million of them through an automatic enrollment push launched in October
  • Children born from 2025 to 2028 get a one-off $1,000 federal contribution, and Michael and Susan Dell have pledged $6.25 billion to give $250 to children in lower- and middle-income ZIP codes

SpaceX will give newly issued shares of its Class A common stock to every American child holding an active Trump Account, with chief executive Elon Musk pledging to match the gift from his own stake. The move doubles a commitment Musk made last month and brings the rocket maker into a fast-growing government-backed savings program for children.

In a statement on Wednesday, the company tied the gift to its long-term mission, saying it is building the infrastructure of the future and wants to make life multiplanetary, and that the next generation of Americans should share in ownership of the business developing those systems. Musk followed up on Thursday with a post on X saying SpaceX would distribute its shares next month, while his personal contribution would be transferred once his lockup period expires in June next year.

The pledge sits alongside an earlier commitment from Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president and chief operating officer, who has said she will donate more than 2 million of her own shares through the program. Her gift is aimed at children aged 11 to 17 from low-income areas, with a focus on communities near her home in central Texas.

The announcement landed a day after the Treasury Department said friends and family had contributed more than $1 billion to individual accounts, lifting total deposits across the program above $9 billion. Close to 70 million accounts have now been opened, more than 60 million of them through an automatic enrollment drive the administration launched in October.

Trump Accounts were created under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in July 2025, and offer tax advantages to holders. Any child under 18 with a valid Social Security number can have one, and those born from the start of 2025 to the end of 2028, a window matching President Trump's second term, receive a one-off $1,000 government contribution.

Philanthropic money has followed. The largest commitment so far is a $6.25 billion pledge from Dell Technologies chief executive Michael Dell and his wife Susan, which will put $250 into the accounts of children living in ZIP codes where the median family income is $150,000 or less.

The SpaceX gift differs from those cash pledges in one important respect: it hands children equity in a single company rather than money to be invested more broadly. How much stock that ultimately represents will depend on how many accounts qualify as active when the shares are issued, a figure the company has not spelled out. With corporate and billionaire pledges multiplying, the question for other large companies is whether a share-based gift becomes the new benchmark. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China's industrial profits jump 20.1% in October as electronics do the heavy lifting
item.description:
The data offers some support for Chinese and wider Asian technology supply-chain stocks, where profits are clearly strongest. Its value as a signal for the broader economy is limited, though, because consumer-facing sectors are still struggling. For commodities, stronger factory earnings are mildly supportive for industrial metals, but persistent property weakness caps the upside for steel-linked inputs such as iron ore. The yuan and China-sensitive currencies such as the Australian dollar are likely to take more direction from tariff headlines than from this release. Any new US or EU trade restrictions would hit the export-dependent firms that drove October's gains.

---

Data post here:

  • China's industrial profits growth speeds up to 20.1% y/y in October

---

China's industrial profits accelerated to 20.1% growth in October, but the surge is driven by electronics and exports while consumer-facing industries struggle, leaving the recovery lopsided and exposed to rising trade risks.

Summary:

  • Profits at China's industrial firms rose 20.1% y/y in October, up from 14.4% in September
  • Profits rose 16% in the first ten months, up from 15.5% for January to September
  • Profits at computer, telecommunications and electronic equipment makers doubled over ten months, while furniture makers' profits fell about 52%
  • Weak domestic demand has pushed firms to rely on overseas markets, raising exposure to trade tensions
  • Beijing has introduced measures to lower borrowing costs, boost liquidity and channel financing to priority sectors, with mixed results so far
  • Possible US and EU tariff increases cloud the outlook for export-driven profit growth

Profit growth at China's industrial firms picked up sharply in October, helped by strength in parts of manufacturing. The gains remain concentrated in a handful of sectors, though, while weak domestic demand continues to hold back the wider economy.

Industrial profits rose 20.1% from a year earlier in October, up from a 14.4% gain in September, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed on Friday, as reported by Reuters. For the first ten months of the year, profits were up 16%, a slight acceleration from the 15.5% pace for January to September.

The headline strength hides a stark divide. Profits at makers of computers, telecommunications and other electronic equipment doubled over the first ten months, a standout performance for the technology hardware sector. At the other end of the scale, furniture makers saw profits fall by more than half. That slump likely reflects how heavily the property downturn and cautious household spending continue to weigh on consumer-facing industries.

Weak domestic demand is pushing many companies to look overseas for growth. That has helped earnings this year, with exports a key source of support for manufacturers, but it leaves them more exposed to trade tensions and geopolitical risk. Concern over possible tariff increases and other trade restrictions, particularly from the United States and the European Union, has raised questions about how long export-led profit growth can last.

Beijing has rolled out a series of measures in recent months to support activity, including steps to lower borrowing costs, add liquidity to the financial system and steer financing towards technology, manufacturing and infrastructure. Analysts say the results have been mixed so far, with soft household demand and lingering stress in the property sector still dragging on the broader recovery.

The figures cover industrial firms with annual revenue of at least 20 million yuan, about $3 million, from their main operations.

The October data suggest Chinese industry can still generate strong profits where demand is robust, particularly in electronics. The challenge for policymakers is spreading that strength to the domestic economy, so that growth depends less on export markets that may become harder to access. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: RBI buys no gold for six months but brings another 60 tonnes home
item.description:
For gold, the RBI's pause matters more than the repatriation. Central bank buying has been one of the pillars of the long rally, and a year without additions from one of the biggest official buyers weakens that support just as prices struggle to find a floor. Moving gold home doesn't affect global supply or demand, though it does underline the trend among central banks of keeping reserves within their own borders. A return to buying by the RBI would be a meaningful positive for sentiment. The rupee is likely to dictate the timing, since the central bank has prioritised currency stability. Future monthly reserve data will show whether buying resumes.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold's downside looks limited because the dollar has already done most of its work, CBA says
  • HSBC flags $3,400 as gold's next big test and says it is too early to call a bottom
  • OCBC sees the Indian rupee strengthening to 92.10 per dollar by end-2027 as oil relief builds

---

India's central bank has added virtually no gold in a year, holding steady at 880 tonnes, but it keeps bringing its bullion home, with about 84% now stored in India as falling prices shrink gold's share of reserves.

Summary:

  • The RBI held 880.52 tonnes of gold at end-September 2026, unchanged from end-March and virtually flat over the year
  • Holdings in India rose to 740.13 tonnes, while those with the Bank of England and the BIS fell to 140.39 tonnes
  • That implies about 60 tonnes were repatriated in the half-year, lifting the domestic share to about 84%
  • The value of the RBI's gold fell to about $106 billion from $115 billion as prices declined
  • Gold's share of India's FX reserves fell to about 14.4% from 16.7%
  • The RBI said rising US yields, a stronger dollar and tighter policy expectations drove gold's roughly 9% price fall over the period

The Reserve Bank of India bought no gold in the six months to the end of September, but it kept bringing its existing bullion home, shifting around 60 tonnes from overseas vaults to domestic storage, according to its latest half-yearly report on foreign exchange reserves (dated November 25).

The RBI held 880.52 tonnes of gold at the end of September, exactly the same as at the end of March and virtually unchanged from a year earlier. Of that total, 740.13 tonnes were held in India, while 140.39 tonnes were in safe custody with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements. Six months earlier, about 680 tonnes were stored domestically and close to 198 tonnes abroad, with a further 2.8 tonnes held as gold deposits.

Based on calculations from the RBI's data, roughly 84% of India's gold reserves now sit at home, up from about 77% at the end of March. In March 2024, less than half was held domestically. The central bank brought home around 168 tonnes in the 2025/26 fiscal year alone, after moving just over 100 tonnes in each of the two previous years.

The repatriation changes where the gold is kept, not how much the RBI owns, so it adds nothing to demand for the metal. The more telling signal for gold markets is the absence of fresh buying. India was among the steady central bank buyers that helped drive gold's long rally. A pause by a buyer of its size takes away one source of support at a time when prices are already under pressure.

The value of the RBI's gold fell to about $106 billion at the end of September from around $115 billion in March, cutting gold's share of India's total foreign exchange reserves to about 14.4% from 16.7%. Prices drove the decline. The RBI said gold averaged about $4,721 an ounce in April and around $4,319 in September, a drop of roughly 9%, as rising US Treasury yields, a stronger dollar and expectations of tighter monetary policy outweighed safe-haven demand.

The pause also fits the RBI's other priorities. The central bank has intervened heavily to support the rupee through a difficult year marked by an oil price shock and capital outflows. With currency stability at the top of its agenda, adding to gold holdings appears to have taken a back seat, even as it continues to secure the bullion it already owns.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: IMF tells RBA to stand ready for more hikes, even after 125bp of tightening this year
item.description:
The IMF's report adds institutional weight to the case against an early end to RBA tightening, which should keep markets wary of pricing in cuts soon. Short-dated Australian government bond yields are the most sensitive to that message. The IMF's explicit link to Middle East energy prices means oil is now a direct input into the RBA debate: a renewed spike in crude would strengthen the hawks' case. For the Australian dollar, a firmer rate outlook offers some support, but global risk sentiment and AI-related equity swings are likely to remain the bigger drivers. The December 8 decision and the next labour market data are the near-term tests.

---

Earlier:

  • Australia's 12% investment surge, the biggest since 2011, keeps RBA hike risk alive: Citi

---

The IMF wants the RBA ready to tighten further if inflation sticks, even though its report was written before the November hike, and it is pressing the government to make sure fiscal policy pulls in the same direction.

Summary:

  • The IMF said the RBA should stand ready to raise rates further if inflation proves more persistent than expected
  • It cited upside risks, including a further escalation of the Middle East war and prolonged high energy prices
  • The IMF warned that inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored after years of above-target inflation
  • The report refers to 100bp of tightening this year, suggesting it predates the November hike that took the total to 125bp
  • The IMF called fiscal consolidation appropriate but said delivering lasting spending restraint is crucial
  • The RBA's next policy decision is due on December 8

The International Monetary Fund has urged the Reserve Bank of Australia to stand ready to raise interest rates further if inflation proves more stubborn than expected, while pressing the government to follow through on its commitments to rein in spending.

In its 2026 Article IV consultation report on Australia, reported by Bloomberg on Friday, the IMF said further monetary tightening would be needed if upside shocks to inflation materialise, including if the war in the Middle East escalates and energy prices stay high for longer. It also warned that, after several years of inflation above target and a run of shocks, inflation expectations risk becoming less well anchored.

The report appears to have been finalised before the RBA's latest move. It refers to 100 basis points of cumulative tightening this year, but the central bank's November hike lifted that total to 125 basis points, taking the cash rate to 4.85%, the highest in 18 years. So the IMF's call for readiness to tighten further comes on top of a hike it had not yet accounted for.

On fiscal policy, the IMF described the shift towards consolidation as appropriate but said delivering on spending restraint is crucial. It said federal and state budgets for 2026/27 are rightly focused on controlling structural spending over the medium term, but more work is needed to lock in lasting savings. The message is that monetary policy should not be left to carry the inflation fight alone.

The IMF's stance lines up with the more hawkish voices on the RBA. Citigroup said this week that domestic demand is now growing faster than the economy's potential after a surge in AI-related business investment. It expects the RBA to hold at 4.85% but sees a risk of further hikes. Not everyone agrees. OCBC argued this week that the RBA is close to the end of its tightening cycle, pointing to a softening labour market, with unemployment at a five-year high of 4.9%.

The RBA's own board was split last time: six members voted for the November hike and three preferred to hold, underlining how finely balanced the decision has become. The bank's next policy announcement is due at 03:30 GMT on December 8 (22:30 US Eastern on December 7). With inflation still above the 2% to 3% target band and the IMF now explicitly backing further tightening if needed, the bar for a pause looks high, even as the jobs market cools.

The Reserve Bank of Australia hiked to 4.85% at its November meeting. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Kiwi edges higher as official NZ election count confirms a hung parliament
item.description:
The muted reaction suggests NZD traders are pricing politics as noise unless talks break down. The tail risk is a failed negotiation and a fresh election, which would bring a longer period of uncertainty and could weigh on the currency and New Zealand government bonds. Coalition deals that come with large fiscal commitments are the other thing to watch, especially for bond yields. Outside Wellington, the kiwi remains tied to global risk sentiment and the US dollar. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December and AI-related volatility still unsettling equities, those forces are likely to outweigh the election result.

---

Earlier:

  • NZ consumer confidence breaks 100 as falling fuel prices cool inflation fears

---

New Zealand's official count has confirmed a hung parliament, but the kiwi's small rise suggests currency traders see coalition talks as a political puzzle rather than an economic threat, at least for now.

Summary:

  • The New Zealand dollar edged higher after official election results confirmed a hung parliament
  • The incumbent centre-right coalition will need the centrist Opportunity Party to govern
  • The small move suggests markets see limited immediate economic risk from coalition talks
  • A prolonged stalemate or a fresh election remains the main political risk for the currency
  • Global risk appetite, the US dollar and the RBNZ outlook are likely to remain the bigger drivers

The New Zealand dollar edged higher on Friday after official election results confirmed a hung parliament. The modest move suggests currency traders see little immediate economic risk in the drawn-out coalition talks that now lie ahead.

The final count from the Electoral Commission left the incumbent centre-right coalition short of a majority on its own, so it will need the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to govern. The result removes some of the uncertainty that hung over the preliminary election-night tally, even if it doesn't yet settle who will form the next government.

The kiwi's gain of a few points was small by any measure, and the lack of a sharper reaction is telling. Political uncertainty in New Zealand rarely moves the currency for long, and markets appear to be treating the result as a question of coalition arithmetic rather than a shift in economic direction. Having a centrist kingmaker, rather than a party on either ideological flank, may also limit concern about abrupt changes to fiscal policy.

The risks haven't disappeared. Negotiations could stretch on for weeks, and if no workable government emerges, New Zealand could face a fresh election. A prolonged stalemate, or a deal that came with significant spending or tax commitments, could test the currency and the local bond market. For now, though, traders seem content to wait.

In the meantime, the kiwi's direction is likely to depend on more familiar drivers. Global risk appetite has been fragile amid turmoil in AI-linked stocks, and the New Zealand dollar, like its Australian counterpart, tends to struggle when investors retreat from risk. The US dollar has been supported by expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Moves in those markets, along with the outlook for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, are likely to matter more for the kiwi in the coming days than developments in Wellington.

Traders will watch for any signs of progress in coalition talks, but unless the politics turn messy, the election looks set to remain a sideshow for the currency. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
